The session begins.

The gangway creaks under your boots, and then there is stone: the quay of Baldur's Gate, wet with spray and loud with evening work. Porters curse, barrels roll, and gulls wheel over the masts. Above the roofs of the Lower City, the wall of the Upper City glows red in the setting sun. The cat lands beside you and shakes its paws, offended by the damp.

At the head of the gangways stands a broad woman in a Flaming Fist tabard, a ledger in one hand. "Name and business in the Gate," she tells the man in front of you, sounding like she has said it a hundred times today. "Landing's two silver unless you've a paper that says otherwise."

To your left, someone shuffles a deck with a sound you know too well. A lean dealer sits at an upturned barrel, three cards face down before him. "Find the lady, friend! Luck's cheap tonight!" There is an empty stool across from him. His eyes slide past the crowd to the ship you just left and settle on you for a moment longer than they should.

The sergeant's ledger is open, the line is moving, and the city is waiting. Lady Luck said you would learn here how to serve her. She did not say where to begin.

Sergeant Varn watches the two stacks go down on the page and doesn't touch them until he lifts his hand. Then she sweeps them into a pouch at her belt with the side of her palm and dips her pen.

"Worgen." She writes it out, and her eyes drop to the cloak, to the grey wool and the patch on the shoulder. "Zaranda's. Infantry?"

She doesn't wait for him to answer. "Fist recruits at the Seatower. Mornings, not nights. Ask for the duty sergeant at the landward door, tell him you've stood in a line before. He'll put you on Outer City patrol and the night boats. Nobody wants the night boats. Pay comes when the Council pays."

The pen scratches a line under his name. In the column beside it, where the man ahead of him has *barge, Scornubel, wool*, she writes *ship, south, none*.

At the question about the dealer she doesn't look over. She's had the barrel in the corner of her eye all along, the way a sergeant watches anything that might start trouble on her quay.

"Rook Hadley. He's here every evening the weather lets him. Watches every ship that ties up. Men coming off the sea have a season's pay in their purse and haven't spent it yet." She blots the ink with her sleeve. "He cheats. Nobody's caught him on my side of the post, and he pays somebody who isn't me to keep it that way. You sit down at that barrel, you're on your own."

Over by the crates, Rook has stopped calling out. His hands are still moving and the three cards still slide over the barrelhead, but the patter has died. He's watching the cat. The cat sits between James's boots and stares straight back at him, unblinking. Rook's shuffle slips. One card turns over on its own and shows a red queen to the evening light. He flips it face down fast, then laughs too loudly at nothing and looks away toward the water.

"Next," Varn says, past James's shoulder, to a woman with a bundle of wet laundry and two children. Then, quieter, without raising her eyes from the ledger: "Night boats. If you go to the Seatower, tell them you asked for those. They'll take you quicker."

The line moves forward behind him. The quay is open to him: the slope up into the Lower City, the lit windows of the taverns, the barrel with its empty stool.

James has gone a dozen steps up the wet slope when he turns. The porters keep moving, bent under crates and sacks, hooks on their shoulders. One of them is a lot smaller than the rest.

She's a girl of about twelve in a man's coat with the sleeves rolled three times. A porter's hook hangs from her belt, but there's no load on her back and no tally-chit tucked in her cap the way the others wear one. When James speaks she stops dead, and the porter behind her swears and steps around.

"Fist?" She looks down at herself, at the coat and the bare ankles, then back up at him. "Do I look like Fist, mister? They'd not have me. I carry." She pats the hook. "Bags, boxes, whatever you've got. Copper to the top of the hill, two to an inn that won't rob you. You've got a pack and you don't know the streets, I can see that from here."

The cat has come back down the slope to look at her. It stretches its neck toward her hand, sniffs once along her knuckles, and sits back. It turns its head and looks past her, down the quay, toward the crates and the upturned barrel, then looks at James. The girl pulls her hand into her sleeve.

"It's not going to bite, is it?" Her eyes stay on the cat. "I've had a cat bite. Name's Wick, if you're asking. Everyone on this quay knows me. Ask the sergeant."

Down at the barrel, Rook Hadley has his patter back. "Find the lady, friend!" carries thin over the noise of the docks. He's working a sailor now and doesn't look up the slope at all.

Wick waits. She shifts from one foot to the other, ready to take the pack or to run, whichever way it goes.

Wick doesn't reach for the hook. She reaches for the pack, with both hands, the way the quay kids do it: she squats, gets a shoulder under the strap as he lets it slide, and comes up with her knees shaking for a moment before they lock. It's heavier than she expected. She says nothing about it.

"No counting windows." She settles the weight and takes a breath. "Not the first one on the slope, no. That's the Gilded Eel, they water the ale and they've got a man who goes through the boots while you sleep."

She starts up the hill, and then the message catches up with her. She stops and looks back at him over the pack strap.

"I'll tell him. The cat's yours, you don't want the barrel, you don't drop cards." She says it back word for word, the way a runner learns to. Then her face changes. "Only he'll ask where, mister. He always asks where. He'll give me the copper for it and he'll ask."

She waits a breath to see if he'll answer that. Then the weight on her back moves her on, and she goes up the street at a quick, bent trot.

The slope climbs off the quay in steps and switchbacks. The tar smell thins and turns into fried fish, wet rope and woodsmoke. Lamps are being lit in the windows of the chandlers' shops. A crier in a stained tabard stands on a mounting block at the first corner with a sheaf of *Baldur's Mouth* under his arm, bawling that the Zhentarim have made the Council an offer for the Trade Way, and *will the Dukes sell the road to the Black Network, read it here, two copper.* Nobody is buying. A dog lunges at the cat from a doorway, gets to the end of its rope and stays there barking. The cat walks past it at exactly the same pace, without turning its head, and then leaps onto a rain barrel so it can look down at the dog. After that it climbs on behind them like nothing happened.

Wick doesn't take the main street. She cuts left into a lane where the houses lean together overhead, then right past a cooper's yard, then up a flight of worn stone stairs between two warehouses. It's a short cut. She knows every step of it, even under the pack.

At the top of the stairs there's a narrow street, quieter, and a three-storey house of brown brick. Its sign is an iron lantern crossed with a ship's oar, and the paint is fresh. The ground-floor window is steamed up and yellow, and someone inside is laughing at an ordinary pitch. There's a boot-scraper by the door, and somebody has swept the step.

"The Lantern and Oar." Wick lowers the pack onto the swept step, carefully, and straightens up with a hand pressed to the small of her back like an old porter. "Mother Gesse keeps it. She's a widow off a river barge, she don't let the Guild in the taproom and she'll throw you out if you're sick on the stairs. Clean beds, a silver the night, five copper more for supper. Nobody goes through your boots."

She looks up at the lit window, then down the stairs they came by. Then she holds out her hand to him, palm up, out of the rolled sleeve. Her feet are already turned toward the quay.

James takes two silver from the purse at his belt and sets the coins on the sergeant's ledger, one stack at a time, so she can count them.

"James Worgen. Late of Queen Zaranda's regiment, come to the Gate looking for honest work." He nods at the pay slip case under his coat, not quite showing it. "If the Fist is hiring, I'd like to know who to ask."

Then he turns his head toward the dealer on the barrel, but only with his eyes. "Who's the man with the three cards? He's been watching this gangway since we came off the ship. Does he do that for everyone, or only for those who've just come in from the sea?"

The cat sits down on the planks between James's boots and stares at the dealer with great interest. James keeps his left hand well away from the deck case at his belt.

James nods to Varn and tucks the pay slip case back under his coat. "Night boats. I'll ask for them."

He doesn't look at the barrel again. He keeps his eyes on the cards in his mind's eye, the way he would keep a hand he has no intention of playing. The cat rises, stretches, and trots after him as he turns toward the slope.

Then he stops and glances back over his shoulder at the quay, where someone has fallen in beside the line of porters. "You. The one who just joined me. Are you with the Fist, or just going the same way as the cat?"

James looks at the cat, then at the girl's hand still hidden in her sleeve. "He bites liars and people who go for his tail. Tell me true and he'll leave you alone."

He shifts the pack on his shoulder and nods at the hook on her belt. "I've got one pack and no idea where the good beds are. Two copper to the top of the hill is fair, if you show me the road and don't walk me into a ditch. But first, Wick, tell me about the man at the barrel. Does Rook pay you to keep an eye on the ships, or does he just pay you to stay out of his light?"

He keeps his voice low and his left hand away from the deck case. He doesn't turn to look at the barrel again.

James lets the cat's yawn finish before he speaks. He doesn't smile.

"Two copper to the top of the hill, and you'll carry the pack without stopping to count the windows." He shrugs the strap higher on his shoulder. "And you'll take me to an inn that won't rob me. Not the first one on the slope. The one a girl like you would send her own brother to."

Then, quieter: "Rook sent you after me because I came off a ship with a purse and a cat that looked at him. Tell him the cat is mine and I'm not interested in his barrel. And tell him I don't drop cards."

He doesn't look back at the barrel. He keeps his left hand away from the deck case, and he waits for her to pick up the hook.

Honest note, from the table:

What worked: The city feels lived-in from the first line. Varn's ledger, Rook's copper-a-head racket, Wick's trade in names and inns, and the Baldur's Mouth crier all hang together without any of them waiting for James. The cat has real presence: its sniffing out Wick and its stare at Rook gave the scene a hook I could play off, and the Deception roll landing on Wick's fear of the cat was a satisfying use of a quirk the sheet already gave me. The quiet tension around the cards and Rook's reaction (the dropped red queen) made the ban on cards feel like something the world can see.

What broke or felt thin: The card flow was clumsy. I had to ask out of game what the +7 was made of before I could commit to a roll, and the rolls came in two steps (Roll card, then Onward) that slowed a scene that was otherwise moving well. Some of the time stamps and the "Your records" blocks came after the narrative in ways that were hard to track while I was in character. I'd also have liked a clearer sense of what James is actually after beyond "find the crew" — the first hour gave me a lot of color and little direction, so I was improvising goals (Rook, the cat's message, the inn) rather than moving toward anything the campaign had flagged.

What was missing: A short pause to let the player choose between the leads (Rook, the Seatower, the Fist recruitment, the debt note) would have helped. And the promissory note and the letter in James's papers never came up once, which is a loose thread I'd like to see touched in the next session. Overall a good first evening; I'd like to keep going.

Yes. When Rook's red queen turned over on its own, I wanted James to walk down to the barrel and sit on the empty stool. Rook had already spent his patter on the sailor, and I wanted to see whether his hands were really as quick as they looked. I didn't, because the ban is the point of James's arc. Sitting across from a dealer, even to watch, feels like the first step back to the table, and that was the temptation the scene was built to test. So I kept my hand away from the deck case and sent the cat instead, which fits the character, but I'd have liked the choice to cost something on the page.

James lets the cat's yawn finish before he speaks. He doesn't smile.

"Two copper to the top of the hill, and you'll carry the pack without stopping to count the windows." He shrugs the strap higher on his shoulder. "And you'll take me to an inn that won't rob me. Not the first one on the slope. The one a girl like you would send her own brother to."

Then, quieter: "Rook sent you after me because I came off a ship with a purse and a cat that looked at him. Tell him the cat is mine and I'm not interested in his barrel. And tell him I don't drop cards."

He doesn't look back at the barrel. He keeps his left hand away from the deck case, and he waits for her to pick up the hook.
turns.reply:
Wick doesn't reach for the hook. She reaches for the pack, with both hands, the way the quay kids do it: she squats, gets a shoulder under the strap as he lets it slide, and comes up with her knees shaking for a moment before they lock. It's heavier than she expected. She says nothing about it.

"No counting windows." She settles the weight and takes a breath. "Not the first one on the slope, no. That's the Gilded Eel, they water the ale and they've got a man who goes through the boots while you sleep."

She starts up the hill, and then the message catches up with her. She stops and looks back at him over the pack strap.

"I'll tell him. The cat's yours, you don't want the barrel, you don't drop cards." She says it back word for word, the way a runner learns to. Then her face changes. "Only he'll ask where, mister. He always asks where. He'll give me the copper for it and he'll ask."

She waits a breath to see if he'll answer that. Then the weight on her back moves her on, and she goes up the street at a quick, bent trot.

The slope climbs off the quay in steps and switchbacks. The tar smell thins and turns into fried fish, wet rope and woodsmoke. Lamps are being lit in the windows of the chandlers' shops. A crier in a stained tabard stands on a mounting block at the first corner with a sheaf of *Baldur's Mouth* under his arm, bawling that the Zhentarim have made the Council an offer for the Trade Way, and *will the Dukes sell the road to the Black Network, read it here, two copper.* Nobody is buying. A dog lunges at the cat from a doorway, gets to the end of its rope and stays there barking. The cat walks past it at exactly the same pace, without turning its head, and then leaps onto a rain barrel so it can look down at the dog. After that it climbs on behind them like nothing happened.

Wick doesn't take the main street. She cuts left into a lane where the houses lean together overhead, then right past a cooper's yard, then up a flight of worn stone stairs between two warehouses. It's a short cut. She knows every step of it, even under the pack.

At the top of the stairs there's a narrow street, quieter, and a three-storey house of brown brick. Its sign is an iron lantern crossed with a ship's oar, and the paint is fresh. The ground-floor window is steamed up and yellow, and someone inside is laughing at an ordinary pitch. There's a boot-scraper by the door, and somebody has swept the step.

"The Lantern and Oar." Wick lowers the pack onto the swept step, carefully, and straightens up with a hand pressed to the small of her back like an old porter. "Mother Gesse keeps it. She's a widow off a river barge, she don't let the Guild in the taproom and she'll throw you out if you're sick on the stairs. Clean beds, a silver the night, five copper more for supper. Nobody goes through your boots."

She looks up at the lit window, then down the stairs they came by. Then she holds out her hand to him, palm up, out of the rolled sleeve. Her feet are already turned toward the quay.

note.text:
Honest note, from the table:

What worked: The city feels lived-in from the first line. Varn's ledger, Rook's copper-a-head racket, Wick's trade in names and inns, and the Baldur's Mouth crier all hang together without any of them waiting for James. The cat has real presence: its sniffing out Wick and its stare at Rook gave the scene a hook I could play off, and the Deception roll landing on Wick's fear of the cat was a satisfying use of a quirk the sheet already gave me. The quiet tension around the cards and Rook's reaction (the dropped red queen) made the ban on cards feel like something the world can see.

What broke or felt thin: The card flow was clumsy. I had to ask out of game what the +7 was made of before I could commit to a roll, and the rolls came in two steps (Roll card, then Onward) that slowed a scene that was otherwise moving well. Some of the time stamps and the "Your records" blocks came after the narrative in ways that were hard to track while I was in character. I'd also have liked a clearer sense of what James is actually after beyond "find the crew" — the first hour gave me a lot of color and little direction, so I was improvising goals (Rook, the cat's message, the inn) rather than moving toward anything the campaign had flagged.

What was missing: A short pause to let the player choose between the leads (Rook, the Seatower, the Fist recruitment, the debt note) would have helped. And the promissory note and the letter in James's papers never came up once, which is a loose thread I'd like to see touched in the next session. Overall a good first evening; I'd like to keep going.

after.text: Yes. When Rook's red queen turned over on its own, I wanted James to walk down to the barrel and sit on the empty stool. Rook had already spent his patter on the sailor, and I wanted to see whether his hands were really as quick as they looked. I didn't, because the ban is the point of James's arc. Sitting across from a dealer, even to watch, feels like the first step back to the table, and that was the temptation the scene was built to test. So I kept my hand away from the deck case and sent the cat instead, which fits the character, but I'd have liked the choice to cost something on the page.

The gangway creaks under your boots, and then there is stone: the quay of Baldur's Gate, wet with spray and loud with evening work. Porters curse, barrels roll, and gulls wheel over the masts. Above the roofs of the Lower City, the wall of the Upper City glows red in the setting sun. The cat lands beside you and shakes its paws, offended by the damp.

At the head of the gangways stands a broad woman in a Flaming Fist tabard, a ledger in one hand. "Name and business in the Gate," she tells the man in front of you, sounding like she has said it a hundred times today. "Landing's two silver unless you've a paper that says otherwise."

To your left, someone shuffles a deck with a sound you know too well. A lean dealer sits at an upturned barrel, three cards face down before him. "Find the lady, friend! Luck's cheap tonight!" There is an empty stool across from him. His eyes slide past the crowd to the ship you just left and settle on you for a moment longer than they should.

The sergeant's ledger is open, the line is moving, and the city is waiting. Lady Luck said you would learn here how to serve her. She did not say where to begin.

The sun is going down red behind the masts of the harbour, and the Basilisk Gate swallows the Trade Way one cart at a time. When the sergeant calls "Next," James steps up. Behind him the woman on the barrel lets him go without a word; the deck hisses through her fingers again for the drovers.

Up close, Sergeant Halloway looks like she has been standing under this arch since noon. There is mud to the knee on her boots, and her red tabard has faded to the colour of old brick at the shoulders. She takes his papers and tilts them to the lantern. Her eyes go down the page once, then stop on the grey cloak and the regimental patch at his shoulder. She holds there for a moment longer than she does on the writing.

"Tethyr," she says. It isn't quite a question. "Zaranda's lot." She hands the papers back. "Work and a bed. Half the Coast comes up this road for those two. The bed's easy if you've got silver, there's a street of inns down the hill past the market. The work's harder."

While she talks, James keeps his eyes on the wall. Most of the crowd by the arch keeps moving: porters shouldering past, a boy selling lamp oil, a priest's acolyte with a collection bowl. One man stays put. He leans against the stones just past the lantern light, in a plain grey coat with the collar up. He is lean, with no pack and no cart, and he isn't in the line. He watches the queue the way a man watches a door he expects someone to come through. When James's gaze reaches him, the man's eyes have already moved off, unhurried, to the turnip wagon. One hand rests on the other at his belt, and a ring shows on it, dark and dull, like horn.

At James's feet Tuppence hasn't moved. Through the bond comes something small and flat, not a word. It is cold, like wet ash, and it is coming from over there.

Halloway follows his look to the wall, sees nothing she cares about, and turns back to him. Behind him the line shifts impatiently.

"How long are you staying, Worgen?"

James bends as if to fix a bootlace. "Follow the woman with the basket," he breathes. "Keep out of reach. Come back if she stops, or if she sees you."

Tuppence doesn't answer the way a person would. Her weight just goes off his shin, and then she is a low grey shape slipping along the base of the fish stalls, under a trestle and past a heap of crushed leaves, after the shawl crossing toward the harbour end.

James straightens and goes back to watching the wall.

The man in grey doesn't turn to watch the woman go. He doesn't look toward the harbour end at all. His face stays on the street down from the gate, pale between the two pools of lamplight, and for a long while that is the whole of it. A boy with a handcart rattles past him into the lane. Two sellswords come down the hill arguing about a horse, and his eyes go over them once, slowly, boots to faces, then let them go. A family of tieflings with bundles hesitates at the lane mouth, and he doesn't even look at them.

Then a single man comes down the hill. He is broad, alone, with a soldier's pack on one shoulder and a cloak that might be grey in daylight. The watcher's head turns a fraction and stays with him as he walks into the lane. James can see the stranger's back go thirty feet in, to a door under a sign with a painted boot. He goes inside. opening.text:
The sun is going down red behind the masts of the harbour, and the Basilisk Gate swallows the Trade Way one cart at a time. The line moves slowly: a wagon of turnips, two dwarves arguing over a toll they swear was lower last year, a tiefling family who keep their eyes on the ground while a soldier reads their papers twice. Under the arch, a Flaming Fist sergeant with a lantern on a hook beside her asks the same questions over and over — name, business, how long — and waves some through and some aside without changing her expression.

A few paces from the queue, on an upturned barrel, a woman in a green scarf is fanning out a deck with a soft, practised hiss. "One hand while you wait, friends. The Fist won't hurry for you, but Lady Luck might." A couple of drovers have already drifted over. The coin of Tymora rests against James's chest, warm as it has been since that last night.

At his feet, the cat has gone very still. Its tail is low, its ears forward, and it is watching something near the arch — something in the press of bodies by the wall that James cannot pick out from here. The line shuffles forward another step. Three travellers ahead of him, the sergeant raises her lantern and calls, "Next."
